sections.h2: Which Johnson County offices handle property tax?
sections.html:
In Johnson County the Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) puts a number on your parcel, the sheriff takes your money, and the county clerk holds the liens and the appeal paperwork. Calling the wrong desk costs a day, so keep the split straight.

County offices cluster at 230 Court Street in Paintsville. The clerk sits in Suite 124 at (606) 789-2557 and is closed Saturdays. The sheriff's page gives (606) 789-3411, and both offices run on a weekday 8 to 4 clock.

Rates are not the PVA's call. The Fiscal Court sits on the second Monday of the month at 4:45 PM, and the county's two public school systems, Johnson County Schools and Paintsville Independent, are among the bodies that levy tax on a bill.

sections.h2: What are the key tax dates for a Johnson County parcel?
sections.html:
Value is struck on January 1, the roll opens for review on the first Monday of May, and bills arrive in the fall. Those dates come from Kentucky law, so they match every other county, but the offices that act on them are Johnson County's own.

The review window lasts 13 days and includes Saturdays. Anything you want changed has to be raised in that window, and the sheriff's discount for early payment ends November 1. Business equipment and other personal property is listed with the PVA through May 15. Ask the sheriff to confirm each year's collection dates, because the state sometimes shifts them.

sections.h2: What happens to an unpaid Johnson County bill?
sections.html:
On April 15 the sheriff hands any unpaid bill to the Johnson County Clerk. The clerk records a lien, and the bill can end up in the hands of a private buyer.

A tax sale cannot come sooner than 90 days after the handoff, under KRS 134.128, and interest of 1 percent a month runs in the meantime. The county attorney writes to the owner, and the clerk publishes the delinquent list before the sale. A county that also sells overdue oil and gas or unmined mineral bills gets 60 extra days, which suits a coalfield county where those interests are billed apart from the surface.

  • The lien rides with the land, so a buyer inherits it unless it is cleared.
  • Whoever buys the bill at the sale can add fees of their own.
  • Letters go to the address on file, so an outdated address means missed warnings.

sections.h2: What is the appeal route for a Johnson County value?
sections.html:
Ask the PVA for a conference in May. No filing with the board is allowed until that meeting has happened, and the PVA must explain how your number was built.

If the meeting settles nothing, file at the clerk's office in time for the following workday. A panel of local property owners hears the case. It must turn down any appeal that shows up without proof, for instance insurance policies, building costs or sales listings.

  • Ask which sales the PVA relied on for your house.
  • Get repair quotes if damage is missing from the record.
  • A paid representative must be an attorney, CPA, licensed appraiser or another category the state recognizes.

Past the local board, the Kentucky Board of Tax Appeals is the last stop. With median values near $120,000, even a few thousand dollars off the value shifts a bill, so the call is worth making.

sections.h2: Who can claim a homestead or other exemption in Johnson County?
sections.html:
A homeowner who is 65 or older, or totally disabled under a federal or retirement plan, can take the homestead and disability deduction. One per household is the limit, and it travels with the owner, so a purchaser has to file fresh.

Kentucky resets the dollar amount every two years. A neighboring-region PVA posts $49,100 for 2025 to 2026, so confirm the Johnson County figure with the PVA. Service-connected totally disabled veterans and people ruled disabled by Social Security or Kentucky Retirement file once, while those classed disabled by an out-of-state agency refile every year.

Churches, schools and charities apply on Revenue Form 62A023. Farmland is taxed on use value, a break the state says can be large where market prices run well above farm prices. Separately from property tax, the county charges an occupational tax of 0.5 percent on wages and net profit earned inside Johnson County.

sections.h2: How does Johnson County housing compare with other Kentucky counties?
sections.html:
Homes cost far less here than in the state's metro counties. Census survey figures for 2020 to 2024 put Johnson County's median home value at $120,200, a number that shapes how much any one assessment change matters to a bill.

Johnson County counted 22,680 people in 2020 and an estimated 22,051 in July 2025, a drop of 2.8 percent. Its population peaked at 25,771 in 1940. The 2020 census found 12.0 percent of the county's 10,493 housing units vacant, against 5.8 percent in Jessamine County and 6.9 percent in Kenton County.

Floodplain rules touch some parcels. Building in a Special Flood Hazard Area needs both a state and a local permit, and the county asks owners to call (606) 789-2550 before any development.

sections.h2: What does the Johnson County landscape look like?
sections.html:
Johnson County covers 264 square miles in the Eastern Coalfield and borders Lawrence, Martin, Floyd, Magoffin and Morgan counties. The highest point is Stuffley Knob at 1,496 feet, and the lowest is the Levisa Fork on the Lawrence County line at roughly 550 feet.

Paintsville is the only city and the seat. Van Lear and West Van Lear are census-designated places, and Paintsville Lake State Park, with a 1,140 acre lake, lies near Staffordsville. Big Sandy Community and Technical College runs two campuses in the county, at Mayo and Hager Hill.

On a rural parcel here, check the access road, the exact acreage and any flood zone before you set a price.

sections.h2: How did Johnson County's coal and oil history shape its parcels?
sections.html:
The railroad reached Paintsville in 1904 and opened the coal era, which lasted more than a century. Consolidation Coal and North East Coal built the towns of Van Lear and Thealka, and by the 1940s as many as 1,500 men worked the county's mines.

Oil and gas followed from 1917, and in 1922 the Johnson-Magoffin field produced over 2,000,000 barrels. Coal output peaked in 2008 at 2,713,196 tons. Wikipedia adds that many residents sold their mineral rights cheaply during the coal boom.

For a seller, that history is practical. Ask the title company whether minerals were severed from the surface on your parcel, and ask the sheriff whether a separately billed mineral or oil and gas tax bill is tied to it.

sections.h2: What should a Johnson County seller confirm before closing?
sections.html:
Three calls cover nearly every surprise: the sheriff for the bill and a payoff, the clerk for any certificate of delinquency, and the PVA for exemption status.

The county lists separate fire and rescue units for Paintsville, Van Lear, West Van Lear and others, and a Kentucky bill can stack school, city, county and fire levies. Ask the sheriff for a line-by-line breakdown. One Kentucky sheriff's FAQ explains that the seller's share is settled with the buyer at closing while the owner of record pays the full bill.

faqs.q: Which office collects Johnson County property tax?
faqs.a: The Johnson County Sheriff, whose office lists (606) 789-3411.

faqs.q: Where is a Johnson County assessment appeal filed?
faqs.a: At the county clerk, 230 Court Street, Suite 124, Paintsville, once the PVA conference is done. The filing falls due the workday after the May review window shuts.

faqs.q: When does an unpaid Johnson County bill move to the clerk?
faqs.a: After April 15. The clerk then carries it as a certificate of delinquency with a lien on record.

faqs.q: Does a Johnson County homeowner get the 65 exemption automatically?
faqs.a: No. The owner applies through the PVA, and the home must be a primary residence.

faqs.q: Who decides Johnson County tax rates?
faqs.a: The taxing bodies on your bill, such as the Fiscal Court and the school districts. The PVA values property and the sheriff collects.
